About the Author

Mayank Mishra is the founder of ThriveXLabs (TXL), where he builds and runs outbound-led sales and demand-generation systems for B2B businesses. He started his career at Garmin, then built and scaled two EdTech platforms on organic growth. Most recently he ran growth for an expert marketplace that reached 12.5k users in three months: over 1,000 consultants onboarded without a big ad budget, and a 46% reply rate across 11,466 cold LinkedIn DMs. He writes about growth, positioning and demand generation for over 7,000 followers on LinkedIn and 13,000 on Substack. He is also the author of The Non-Salesy DM.

My Story: I'm Not a LinkedIn Influencer, and That's the Point

Let me be upfront about something most LinkedIn books won't tell you.

I'm not a LinkedIn celebrity. I don't have hundreds of thousands of followers. Most of my posts reach a few hundred people. If you bought this book hoping to learn how to get a million impressions, I'm the wrong author, and it's the wrong book.

What I have done is build demand. I've scaled two EdTech platforms on organic growth. And this year I ran growth for an expert marketplace that reached 12.5k users in three months. We onboarded over a thousand consultants without spending millions on ads. The first 1,000 sign-ups took months. The next 1,000 came in seven days.

That work put me in an unusual position. I wasn't just writing posts. I was watching hundreds of consultants, coaches and freelancers try to turn their LinkedIn content into clients, and I could see which ones actually got booked.

Here's what I saw, over and over:

The people getting clients were rarely the people getting the most likes.

The consultant whose inspirational post got 2,000 reactions often had an empty calendar. Meanwhile, one expert on the platform added a booking link to a single, specific LinkedIn post, a post that clearly explained one problem for one kind of buyer, and got a booking from it. No funnel. No sequence. No virality. The right person read it, recognized their problem, checked the profile, and acted.

That's the whole book in one story.

Why I Wrote This Book

Most LinkedIn content advice is built around one number: reach. Hooks to stop the scroll. Formats that "the algorithm loves." Templates that went viral for someone else. Some of that craft is genuinely useful, and you'll find the best of it in these pages.

But reach is the wrong finish line. I've written it in my own notes more times than I can count: reach, likes and impressions are leaky buckets. A viral post is a crowd that gathers for ten seconds. What matters is whether any of them walk somewhere afterward.

And most founders I work with don't have a lead-generation problem. They have a relevance problem. They're getting attention from people who will never buy, while the few people who would buy can't tell what they do.

So this book makes a different promise:

You don't need millions of followers to generate serious business from LinkedIn. You need to consistently earn attention from the right people, show that you understand their problem, and give them a reason to start a conversation.

That's what I call qualified attention, and it's what this book teaches you to build: an engine that turns useful posts into relevant conversations, and relevant conversations into clients.

It pairs with my other book, The Non-Salesy DM. That one covers what happens once a conversation starts. This one covers how the right conversations start in the first place.

Mayank Mishra
Founder, ThriveXLabs

How to Use This Book

The system in one page. Two linked frameworks run through the whole book:

  • V.I.R.A.L. is the work inside a post: Voice (sound like a human who understands the work), Intrigue (earn the next line), Relevance (make the right reader see themselves), Authority (give them grounds to believe you), Lesson (leave them better equipped to act).
  • L.E.A.D. is the work after the post: Lead (create a reason to continue the relationship), Engagement (start a real exchange), Alignment (check whether your help fits), Discovery (move the right people into a business conversation).

Every post is built on one architecture: Hook → Rehook → Body → Payoff → CTA. And one editing checklist, V.A.L.U.E. (Visibility, Attention, Legitimacy, Usefulness, Engagement-to-Action), is your final pass before you publish.

How to read it.

  1. Parts I–IV in order: they change what you write about and why.
  2. Part V to build your operating system.
  3. Keep Part VI (the Playbook: hooks, rehooks, post structures and annotated examples) open while you write.

What comes with this edition. The Implementation System: the Content Engine Tracker (a spreadsheet with a problem bank, post planner, proof ledger, 50-hook bank, 30-day challenge and honest metrics), the AI Post Coach (turns a buyer problem into briefs, hooks and drafts using this method, without ever inventing your experience), and the printable Field Kit.

A note on evidence. This book's frameworks are practical writing and planning tools, not discoveries about LinkedIn's ranking algorithm, and nothing here guarantees reach or revenue. The concept behind the book drew on a large study of viral LinkedIn posts. Its underlying dataset and method weren't available for verification, so I don't cite its numbers as proof. Where I describe what LinkedIn has said about its feed, I cite LinkedIn directly. Named businesses, figures and first-person stories in the teaching examples are illustrative unless I say they're mine. Where I use openings from my own posts, I say so.

The one rule for the whole book: optimize for qualified attention, not maximum attention.

Part I · The Virality Reset

Chapter 1: Stop Chasing Viral

Don't maximize attention. Maximize valuable attention.

Two posts from the same consultant, one week apart.

Post A is a story about perseverance: the year everything went wrong and what it taught her. Thousands of people recognize themselves in it. 80,000 impressions. 1,900 reactions. 300 comments, most of them some version of "So needed this today."

Post B explains why agency proposals stall after a verbal "yes": usually because nobody owns the internal decision. 4,000 impressions. 60 reactions. 11 comments. Two of those comments are agency founders describing that exact problem in their own business. One sends a DM that becomes a paid project.

(Illustrative example.)

By every number on the dashboard, Post A won. By the only number that pays for anything, Post B won. And the consultant's natural reaction, "write more posts like A," is exactly the wrong lesson.

Viral ≠ valuable

Most people believe LinkedIn content has one job: get engagement. That belief quietly shapes everything: the topics you pick, the hooks you write, the posts you repeat.

But a post can be widely shared because it's funny, moving, controversial or culturally familiar. None of those qualities tells you whether its readers have a problem you solve. Reach creates possibilities. Audience, meaning and the next step decide which possibilities are useful.

Vanity LinkedIn vs. Business LinkedIn
Vanity LinkedIn optimizes for… Business LinkedIn optimizes for…
More impressions More relevant impressions
More likes More authority with the right people
More followers More profile visits from potential buyers
More comments More qualified conversations
A viral post Opportunities, and eventually revenue

A viral post is a crowd that gathers for ten seconds. The engine is what decides whether any of them walk somewhere afterward.

The two equations

It helps to think of it this way:

Viral content ≈ Attention × Relevance × Value × Emotion × Distribution
Qualified leads ≈ Reach × Audience fit × Authority × Problem awareness × Trust × Conversion path

Figure 1. The two equations. They're diagnostic reminders, not arithmetic. The terms don't share units.

The point isn't to calculate anything. It's that the second equation contains every weak link that more reach can't fix:

  • The wrong people respond? Fix audience fit and topic.
  • The right people read but can't explain what you do? Fix authority and positioning.
  • Readers ask good questions but never progress? Fix the conversion path: your offer, your next step, your replies.

More impressions can't repair any of those. That's why doubling your reach so often doubles the noise, not the pipeline.

Qualified attention

This book's central unit is qualified attention: attention from people whose situation makes your expertise relevant.

Some of them will buy. Some will influence a purchase, introduce you to someone, or remember you months later. Others will learn something useful and leave. A good engine serves all of them honestly, while making the commercial path obvious to the right ones.

The goal isn't to get 100,000 people to like your post. It's to get the right 100 to 1,000 people to think: "This person understands my problem. I should talk to them."

Define useful success before you write

Give every post one primary job:

  • Attraction: introduce a relevant idea to new, relevant people.
  • Authority: make your thinking more credible.
  • Relationship: deepen understanding or invite worthwhile discussion.
  • Conversion: help an appropriate reader take a defined next step.

Then judge the post by its job. Don't change the definition of success after you publish. If a conversion post earns likes but no interest in the offer, the likes don't retroactively become the goal. And if an authority post helps one real prospect resolve an objection, low reach doesn't make it a failure. (Chapter 12 turns these four jobs into a posting mix.)

A qualified opportunity is much more demanding than an interaction. In this book it means an identifiable person or organization with a relevant problem, a plausible fit with your offer, a credible path to a decision, and an agreed next step. A download is not an opportunity. A complimentary comment is not an opportunity.

The transformation

You start as someone who asks "What should I post?" By the end of this book you'll know:

  1. How to create attention
  2. How to create authority
  3. How to attract your ideal buyer specifically
  4. How to run a repeatable content system that produces conversations and leads

It's less a writing book than a LinkedIn demand-generation playbook that happens to be about writing.

Action: your content objective

Write one sentence:

"Over the next 30 days, I want [specific audience] to recognize [specific problem] and consider [appropriate next step]."

Then list three signals of progress you can actually observe (relevant replies, resource use, substantive DMs, fit conversations) and one commercial outcome you'll track over a longer period.

  • ☐ One primary audience is named.
  • ☐ The problem is specific enough to recognize in a real conversation.
  • ☐ The next step is useful even if the reader never buys.
  • ☐ Success includes audience quality, not reach alone.
Field rule: A post that reaches 4,000 of the right people beats one that reaches 80,000 of the wrong ones.

Chapter 2: What Viral Posts Can (and Can't) Teach You

Study the decisions behind a post, not its surface.

Studying successful posts is useful when you study decisions: how the writer introduced a problem, set the stakes, supplied evidence and rewarded the reader. It's much less useful when you copy surface patterns and assume they caused the result.

The survivorship trap

A dataset made up only of viral posts can tell you what appears among viral posts. Without a comparison group, it can't tell you whether the same features appear in thousands of ignored posts too.

If most winning posts use "I" and "you," that doesn't prove adding "I" creates reach. The author's audience, topic, timing, reputation and existing distribution all explain part of the difference. Personal, conversational writing is very often good writing. Just don't mistake a correlation in winners for a lever you can pull.

The research quality filter

Before you adopt any "LinkedIn study says…" claim, ask:

  • Who collected the data, and when?
  • How were posts selected? What counted as "viral"?
  • Was paid promotion excluded?
  • Did it compare similar authors and topics?
  • Was the outcome reach, engagement, leads or revenue? (These are not interchangeable.)

The large viral-post study behind this book's original concept couldn't pass this check, because its dataset and method weren't available to me. You don't need to wait for perfect research to write better posts. You do need to stop treating unverified figures as proof, including the ones in viral threads about LinkedIn itself.

What LinkedIn has actually said

LinkedIn has publicly described feed changes intended to favor relevant professional content and reduce generic, recycled posts and engagement bait (empty "agree?" or "comment YES" prompts). It has also said it acts against engagement pods and automated comments as inauthentic activity.

That supports a sensible emphasis on relevance and substance. It does not reveal a dependable trick for making any particular post travel. And none of it establishes a universal best posting time, a mandatory "first-hour" reply window, an ideal line count, or a guaranteed penalty for every external link. Treat those claims as hypotheses to test, not laws.

Craft principles vs. ranking guesses

Craft principle (helps readers) Ranking guess (treat as a hypothesis)
Short paragraphs make a dense argument easier to scan "Short lines get boosted"
A personal scene makes an abstract issue concrete "Stories always go viral"
A clear opening helps the reader decide to continue "The first line is all the algorithm reads"
Put a link where it best serves the reader "Links always kill reach"

External links are a good example of confused reasoning. A link asks readers to leave the feed, so posts with links may perform differently. That alone doesn't prove an algorithmic penalty. Put the link where it serves the reader, test for your own objective, and never bury an essential resource just to obey folklore.

Give good work a realistic route to readers

Distribution starts before you publish:

  • Connect with people whose work you can contribute to. A smaller network with shared professional context beats a large pile of unrelated contacts. Don't send connection requests that hide a prepared pitch. (That's the whole subject of The Non-Salesy DM.)
  • Comment like a contributor. Add an example, a useful distinction or a well-formed question. "Great post!" repeated across the feed gives nobody a reason to look at your work.
  • Make posts easy to pass along privately. Ask: who would send this to whom, and what sentence would they write when they did? "Our team needs to decide this before the launch" is a much stronger distribution reason than "this person wants reach."
  • Use your existing channels honestly. Reference a relevant post in your newsletter or in an agreed client follow-up. Never ask a group to simulate independent enthusiasm. That's a pod, and pods are exactly what LinkedIn says it acts against.
  • Collaborate with substance. A joint post between a sales-process consultant and an agency operations lead can expose trade-offs neither would explain alone. Agree the topic, permissions and credit first.

For new accounts: the first problem is usually limited exposure, not weak writing. Spend part of your first month finding where your buyers already discuss the problem, and participate usefully there. Don't treat low early reach as proof you need a more sensational hook.

Build your own small evidence base

Your best data is your own. Review ten of your posts with a similar audience and purpose. Record topic, format, opening, proof, CTA, reach, relevant responses and opportunities. Look for patterns, then test one change across several comparable posts.

Don't call a three-post difference conclusive. And if you're starting from zero, build a baseline instead of borrowing someone else's. Those early conversations are research even when the analytics look flat.

Action: audit one "rule"

Pick one popular LinkedIn writing rule you currently follow. Write down:

  1. The claim
  2. Its source
  3. An alternative explanation for why it might seem to work
  4. A practical test

Replace "LinkedIn always rewards this" with "I'll test whether this helps my readers and my objective."

Field rule: Copy decisions, not decorations.

Chapter 3: The Anatomy of a Useful Post

Hook → Rehook → Body → Payoff → CTA.

Every useful LinkedIn post has a coherent movement. These are functions, not boxes of equal size. A short post may combine several in one sentence. A case study may need room to set up context before its lesson is believable.

Hook
Stop the right readerRehook
Make the next line necessaryBody
Deliver the story or valuePayoff
Resolve the promiseCTA
A proportionate next step

Figure 2. The Attention Architecture, the structure used throughout this book.

When one part contradicts another (a big hook with a thin body, a helpful post with a pushy CTA), the post feels manipulative even if every sentence is polished.

A complete miniature

Your proposal may be waiting for a decision nobody owns.

Before rewriting the pricing page, check what happened after the last call.

Was one person responsible for taking the recommendation to their team? Was there a date for that conversation? Did you agree what the other decision-makers would need?

"They liked the proposal" is a reaction.
"The ops lead reviews scope with the founder on Thursday" is a next step.

On your next sales call, finish by confirming the decision, the owner and the date. If any of them is unknown, write that down instead of treating the deal as close to won.

Which of those three is usually missing in your pipeline?

Function What it does here
Hook Names a specific, recognizable failure
Rehook Redirects from the familiar response (rewrite the price) to the real check
Body Three questions the reader can run on their own pipeline
Payoff A memorable contrast (reaction vs. next step) plus one concrete habit
CTA Invites relevant experience, not agreement

The promise–payoff contract

Before drafting, write the promise in plain language: "This post will help an agency owner tell a pricing objection apart from an unclear decision process." Then check every paragraph against it.

  • If the hook promises a pricing diagnosis and the body turns into a speech about confidence, the contract is broken.
  • If the hook promises five steps, deliver five usable steps.
  • If it implies measured results, show the measurement context.

Never withhold the promised answer to force a DM. Give the insight publicly. Offer a resource or service that makes implementation easier, broader or more tailored. Readers can tell the difference between a post that teaches and a post that teases, and only one of them builds authority.

V.I.R.A.L. inside the post

The architecture tells you the order. V.I.R.A.L. tells you what each part must contain:

Question to ask Lives mostly in…
Voice Does this sound like a person who understands the work? Everywhere
Intrigue Would the right reader need the next line? Hook, rehook
Relevance Would my buyer recognize themselves? Hook, body
Authority What here gives them grounds to believe me? Body
Lesson What can they now do or decide? Payoff

After the post, L.E.A.D. takes over (Chapters 13–17): create a reason to continue (Lead), start a real exchange (Engagement), check fit (Alignment), and move the right people into a business conversation (Discovery).

Match the format to the reader's task

  • Text for an argument, a short story or a focused explanation.
  • A simple image for a comparison or diagnostic people grasp at a glance.
  • A document (carousel) post when a sequence benefits from separate pages.
  • Video when a demonstration or spoken explanation is materially clearer.

These are communication choices, not rankings of algorithmic superiority. Design for legibility: one main idea per visual, readable labels, real contrast. A tiny spreadsheet screenshot isn't proof if nobody can read it.

Action: five sentences first

Write one sentence for each of the five functions. Expand only the body until it delivers the promised lesson. Then read the hook and the payoff one after the other. They should make a sensible pair on their own.

Field rule: The hook makes a promise. The body keeps it. Don't write checks the post can't cash.

Part II · The Post Machine

Chapter 4: The Hook

Win the first two seconds with the right reader, not every reader.

The opening line has one job: help a suitable reader recognize either their situation or an interesting implication. It doesn't need to shout louder than every other post. It needs to make the next sentence worth the right person's effort.

A hook needs three things:

  1. A subject: what this is about.
  2. A reason to care: why it matters to someone.
  3. Enough specificity not to sound interchangeable.

"Marketing has changed" has a subject and nothing else. "Your demo-request form may be filtering out the buyers with real urgency" has a problem, a mechanism and an obvious person who should care.

Eleven ways to open

Type What it does Example
Problem Names an observable difficulty "Your proposals go quiet after procurement joins."
Curiosity Opens a meaningful gap "The busiest stage in your CRM may be the least understood."
Contrarian Challenges a belief, with a boundary "More discovery questions can make a simple purchase harder."
Personal story Starts at the decision or consequence "I rewrote the offer before checking who was reading it."
Transformation Contrasts a real before and after "The handoff went from a Slack message to a named owner and deadline."
How I Reveals a process you actually use "How I turn one buyer objection into three useful posts."
Mistake Identifies a correctable action "A common proposal mistake: explaining scope before confirming who decides."
Confession Admits a relevant misconception "I used to treat every resource request as a sales lead."
Data Leads with a supported finding "In our last 40 inquiries, one question came up 23 times." (only with real, sourced numbers)
Prediction A reasoned forecast with conditions "If buyers can compare your process before a call, discovery calls need a new job."
Direct address Names the reader and circumstance "Agency founders who still approve every proposal: read this before hiring another salesperson."

From my own feed

Here are openings from posts I've written, so you can see these types in a real voice:

  • Problem / reframe: "Most freelancers don't have an income problem. They have a pipeline problem."
  • Contrarian: "We chase reach as if it were the finish line, then wonder where the revenue went."
  • Scene: "'Can we just have a quick call?' Every consultant has heard this one."
  • How I: "Here's how I'd market a startup with a $0 ad budget…"
  • Confession (with humor): "Nothing keeps a growth marketer humble like a dashboard."
  • Research: "I analyzed 100+ AI tools, consultant workflows, founder recommendations and AI communities to answer one question…"
  • Comparison: "There are 2 types of AI consultants on our platform right now. (And only one of them consistently gets businesses interested.)"
  • Personal story: "If you only saw my job titles, you'd miss the story."

Notice that each one tells a specific reader, like a freelancer, a consultant or a founder, that this post is for them.

The 15-word test

Try expressing your hook's core idea in 15 words or fewer. This is a compression exercise, not a LinkedIn rule. If the shorter version drops an essential qualifier or becomes misleading, keep the qualifier.

Draft ten hooks before choosing one. Vary the angle, not the adjectives: the symptom, the consequence, the decision, the common response, the overlooked constraint, the evidence, the misconception, an example, a question, a practical promise. Then pick the one most clearly connected to the body.

Repair the overclaim

Weak Better Why
"This one trick will double your leads." "Before posting more, check whether buyers can tell what you sell." A smaller promise you can actually deliver
"Nobody talks about this sales secret." "A signed proposal still needs a clear handoff into delivery." Removes fake exclusivity; makes the issue concrete
"I almost lost everything." "I sent the proposal before confirming who would approve it." True and relevant beats dramatic and vague

A hook that needs exaggeration to stay interesting is telling you the idea underneath is weak. Strengthen the idea.

Action: ten hooks, two finalists

For your next post, write ten hooks across different angles. Score each as clear / partly clear / unclear on three things: audience, problem and deliverability (can the body keep this promise?). Discard any that need exaggeration. Take two finalists to one person in your audience and ask what they expect the post to explain.

Field rule: A great hook makes the right reader stop and the wrong reader keep scrolling. Both are wins.

Chapter 5: The Rehook

Most people obsess over line one. Experts engineer lines one to three as a unit.

The rehook is the sentence or short passage right after the hook that makes the opening worth continuing. On LinkedIn it usually decides whether someone taps "…see more." It's one of the most under-taught skills in post writing.

HookTensionCuriosity"…see more"

A good rehook adds information. Repeating the hook in more dramatic language only delays the answer.

I almost quit my business.

Not because it was failing.

Because it was succeeding in the wrong way.

The second and third lines turn a generic confession into a specific, intriguing tension: what does succeeding the wrong way mean? Now "see more" is an informed choice. (Use this shape only for a true story.)

Consider: "Your marketing report can improve while your pipeline gets weaker." A useful rehook: "That happens when the dashboard rewards activity your buyers don't use to decide." It names a mechanism. "You won't believe what happens next" adds nothing.

Three dependable moves

  • Narrow: "This matters most when the founder still approves every proposal." It helps the right reader recognize themselves, and lets everyone else leave without wasting their time.
  • Complicate: "The team may be following the process exactly. The process may be missing the decision." It earns attention by improving the diagnosis, not by adding suspense.
  • Preview: "Here are three places to check before you change your price." It sets an honest expectation and a clear scope.

You can combine them. But don't build a five-line runway for a two-line insight. If the opening takes longer than the lesson, compress.

Design for the visible opening, without gaming it

How much of a post shows before "see more" varies by device, format and interface, so don't assume a fixed number of lines. Make your first short passage make sense on its own, and preview it in the interface you publish from.

Don't withhold the entire topic. A mystery opening earns curiosity from people who have no reason to care, and frustrates the ones who do. The rehook should give enough context that clicking "see more" is an informed yes.

Worked repair

  • Draft: "I made a huge mistake. It cost me everything. Here's what happened." Unless every word is true and relevant, this is inflated and empty.
  • Revision (true experience): "I sent the proposal before confirming who would approve it. The next two calls repeated a conversation I thought we'd finished." Now the reader knows the situation, the consequence and the likely lesson.
  • Revision (no personal story available): "Sending a proposal before you know who approves it creates an avoidable risk: you may be presenting the answer to someone who still needs help framing the problem." That's an argument, not a fabricated memory. Both work.

Action: three rehooks per hook

For your chosen hook, write three rehooks: one that narrows, one that complicates and one that previews. Pick the one that adds the most meaning. Read the hook and rehook aloud together, and cut any line that could be pasted under twenty unrelated hooks.

Field rule: The hook earns a glance. The rehook earns the read.

Chapter 6: The Seven Post Engines

Choose the engine by your material, not your mood.

An engine is a reusable way of organizing a useful idea. It cuts the number of decisions you need to make before you start writing. It doesn't replace the idea, the evidence or the audience. And the same engine can attract, build authority or convert, depending on its subject and next step.

The Seven Engines at a Glance
Engine Use when you have… Structure Lead potential
1. Story A real sequence of events that clarifies a decision Situation → tension → choice → consequence → interpretation High: shows how you think in situations buyers recognize
2. How-to A bounded task the reader can perform Outcome → prerequisites → steps → quality check → limit High: shows usefulness; leads naturally to implementation help
3. List Distinct signals, mistakes or checks Unifying rule → genuinely different items → priority Medium–high: great for diagnostics
4. Contrarian A familiar recommendation that fails under clear conditions Common advice → missing assumption → counterexample → better rule → boundary High: signals judgment
5. Trend A verified current change affecting a buyer decision Source → what changed → implication → what to check Medium: timely, but perishable
6. Lessons learned A genuine change in how you think Old belief → evidence → revision → application High: credible and human
7. Conversation A real open question for people with experience Context → your current view → specific question Medium: builds relationships and research

Engine 1 · Story

Use a story when a real sequence of events makes a decision easier to understand. The lead potential comes from showing how you think, in circumstances your buyers recognize.

Example: a genuine account of discovering that a delayed project had no internal owner: what you first assumed, what changed your diagnosis, what you did differently. Don't stretch one incident into a universal law.

Template: "We expected [outcome]. Then [observable event] happened. We considered [options] and chose [action] because [constraint]. The result was [supported outcome]. The lesson applies when [boundary]."

Engine 2 · How-to

Use a how-to when the reader needs to complete a bounded task.

Example: "Before your next proposal, write down the decision owner, the review date and the evidence each reviewer needs. Confirm the unknowns on the call. Put the agreed next action in your recap." Specific enough to try today.

Template: "To [task], first check [prerequisite]. Do [step], then [step]. You'll know it's ready when [test]. If [constraint], use [alternative] instead."

Engine 3 · List

Use a list for distinct items with a unifying rule. Don't split one idea into ten near-duplicates to make the headline look substantial.

Example: Three signs your lead magnet is attracting the wrong audience: most requests come from peers outside your market; follow-up questions are about a different problem; people can't say when they'd use the resource. Each one points to a different repair.

Template: "[Number] signs of [specific condition]. [Signal] means check [cause]. Start with [priority rule]."

Engine 4 · Contrarian

Use this when a popular recommendation breaks under identifiable conditions. Its commercial value comes from better judgment, not controversy.

Example: "Post every day" is poor advice for a consultant whose best material comes from delivery work but whose schedule can't support thoughtful daily writing. Three strong posts a week may produce better material and leave time to answer buyers.

Template: "[Advice] makes sense when [condition]. It breaks down when [constraint]. In that situation, choose [alternative] because [mechanism]."

Engine 5 · Trend

Use a trend only when a current change affects a decision your audience has to make. Verify the source. Separate what happened from what you predict. Don't summarize the announcement. Translate it into a decision.

Template: "[Source] announced [change] on [date]. For [reader], the practical question is [decision]. Check [factor] before [action]. My expectation is [inference], especially if [condition]."

Engine 6 · Lessons learned

Use this when you can honestly compare your old model with your current one. It's often more credible than presenting yourself as someone who never got anything wrong.

Example: learning that a polished dashboard doesn't resolve conflicting definitions of a "qualified lead," and that you now agree the definitions before building any report.

Template: "I used to prioritize [choice]. After [real evidence], I now check [factor] first. That changes [action]. I still use the old approach when [exception]."

Engine 7 · Conversation

Use a conversation post to investigate a real question with people who have relevant experience. Give enough context to make a good answer possible, share your own view, and say what would change it.

Example: "For agency owners with a dedicated account manager: which decisions still reach you every week? I'm especially curious about scope changes versus client escalations."

Template: "In [context], I see a choice between [A] and [B]. My current view is [reasoned position]. What have you seen when [specific condition]?"

Choose by material

If you have… Use the…
A sequence of events Story
A repeatable task How-to
A cluster of distinct signals List
A flawed popular assumption Contrarian
A verified change Trend
A revised belief Lessons learned
An open question Conversation

Action: one problem, seven premises

Take one buyer problem and write a one-sentence premise for all seven engines. Choose the two where your material is strongest. Save the rest as research questions rather than forcing seven thin posts into your calendar.

Field rule: The engine organizes the idea. It can't replace one.

Chapter 7: Write Like a Person Who Understands the Work

Voice isn't slang. It's specificity about people, decisions and consequences.

"Human" writing doesn't mean casual slang, deliberately broken grammar or a personal confession in every opening. A precise explanation often sounds more human than a manufactured story.

Corporate abstraction hides the work. "We empower scalable stakeholder alignment" tells the reader nothing. "Before the project starts, we agree who approves changes and how fast they need to respond" describes something a buyer can picture, and evaluate.

Edit at three levels

  • Idea: What changes for the reader after reading this?
  • Paragraph: What does each paragraph contribute? Cut any that don't.
  • Sentence: Replace vague subjects and verbs with concrete ones.

Before: "It is important to ensure that effective communication is prioritized."
After: "Send the client a weekly note: work completed, decisions blocked, next deadline."

The second version can be acted on, and challenged. That's what makes it credible.

Rhythm: short sentences land a decision. Longer ones show a condition or relationship. A post made entirely of clipped one-line declarations becomes monotonous and theatrical. Mix them.

Strong views, honest boundaries

"Always," "never" and "everyone" usually mean the draft has outrun the evidence. Replace them with the actual conditions. "A weekly review helps when several people depend on the same decision" is less dramatic than "Every company needs this meeting," and far more useful.

You can hold a strong point of view without pretending there are no exceptions: state the recommendation, explain why, and name the condition that would change it. That matters most when your reader knows their own business better than you do.

Use AI as an editor, not an author

Give your assistant the audience, the thesis, your source notes, the facts you're allowed to use and a sample of your voice. Ask it to find vague claims, missing steps and unsupported numbers before you ask for a rewrite. And explicitly prohibit invented clients, experiences, quotes and results:

"Preserve these facts. Flag anything that needs evidence. Suggest three clearer openings. Do not add experiences, clients or results."

You're still responsible for the final draft. A fluent paragraph can misrepresent a source or imply a result you never achieved. Keep confidential client information out of tools that aren't approved for it. Anonymizing a name doesn't help if the project, dates and figures are distinctive. (The AI Post Coach in the Implementation System is built around exactly these rules.)

Action: the abstraction hunt

Highlight every abstract noun in a draft. Replace at least five with an actor, an action or an observable result. Then delete any sentence that praises the idea without explaining it.

Field rule: If a buyer can't picture it, they can't buy it.

Chapter 8: Stories That Help Buyers Decide

A story earns its place when the event teaches something relevant.

The reader doesn't need your biography. They need enough context to understand the choice, enough tension to care and enough evidence to trust your interpretation.

Start near the decision. "The project was approved, but nobody could name who was responsible for system access" is much closer to the problem than a paragraph about your passion for operational excellence.

The decision story

Build any story from five questions:

  1. What was supposed to happen?
  2. What made it difficult?
  3. What options existed?
  4. Why was one chosen?
  5. What changed, and what's still uncertain?

This exposes your judgment, which is what buyers are really evaluating. It avoids the common pattern where the author appears, applies a mysterious framework and produces a remarkable result without ever explaining the work.

The team wanted a faster proposal template.

But the template was already short. The delay happened before anyone opened it.

Every non-standard request went to the founder. Nobody knew which changes an account lead could approve.

A better template might save writing time. It wouldn't remove the approval queue.

The first repair was a decision rule: which changes the account lead can approve, which need review, and what the reviewer needs to see.

Before speeding up a document, check the decision that comes before it.

Illustrative story. It demonstrates a mechanism without claiming a real client result.

Protect the evidence chain

For real cases, keep the starting state, what you did, the time period, how you defined the outcome, and anything else that changed. If inquiries rose while pricing and paid distribution also changed, don't credit the content rewrite alone. If a client gave you a number you didn't verify, attribute it to them.

Ask permission before using client names, screenshots, quotes or distinctive details. Without permission, use a clearly labeled composite or a generic process example. Never quietly merge several clients into one apparently real success story.

Emotion belongs in the consequence

Frustration, uncertainty, relief and pride help readers understand why a decision mattered, but the emotion should come from the situation, not from declarations that a routine mistake "destroyed everything." For a founder, being the only person who can approve work means interrupted evenings. For an operations lead, a vague handoff means taking the blame for a delay they couldn't prevent. Those stakes are believable because they're attached to a real workflow.

Action: a 200-word decision story

Write a story about a real professional decision in 200 words. Underline the evidence. Circle the interpretation. Add one sentence about where your lesson might not apply. If fact and interpretation blur together, revise before publishing.

Field rule: Buyers don't hire the hero of a story. They hire the judgment inside it.

Part III · From Attention to Authority

Chapter 9: The Right-Person Principle

A great post doesn't appeal to everyone. It makes your ideal buyer feel unusually understood.

Instead of: "5 ways to improve your marketing."
Write: "5 things SaaS founders should stop doing if their pipeline depends on founder-led sales."

The second one has a smaller audience. It also has a far better one, and that's exactly what we want.

Broad → Specific → Commercially relevant

Broad Specific Commercially relevant
"Better marketing" "More consistent inquiries for B2B consultants" "Why inquiries from your lead magnet don't match the service you sell"
"Leadership lessons" "Delegation for agency founders" "Which approvals your account leads should own before you hire another salesperson"
"Financial tips for startups" "Cash planning for seed-stage SaaS" "The three numbers your board will ask about 9 months after your seed round"
"Career advice" "Interview prep for product managers" "How senior PM candidates lose the offer in the case-study round"

The final column sits right next to a decision the reader has to make, which is where buying begins.

Commercial relevance doesn't mean every post mentions your offer. It means the problem territory connects to work you can credibly help with. A thoughtful post on an adjacent topic can build relationships, but a feed dominated by unrelated topics makes your commercial identity hard to remember.

Start with one audience

An audience definition is only useful when it changes what you write. "Entrepreneurs who want growth" is too broad to decide anything. "Owners of B2B service agencies whose proposals still need founder approval" points you toward recognizable situations, relevant examples and a plausible service.

Pick one primary audience for your first 30-day cycle. It's a publishing focus, not a permanent ban on other clients. Changing the buyer, the problem and the offer every week makes your results impossible to read.

The buyer situation statement

"I help [role and business context] dealing with [observable problem] when [trigger or constraint], so they can [valuable change]."

Then add who is outside scope.

Example: "I help owners of small B2B agencies whose sales still depend on their daily involvement build clearer qualification, proposal and follow-up routines." Outside scope: businesses without a validated offer; companies wanting outsourced high-volume prospecting.

Company size, geography and industry matter only when they change the problem, the purchasing process or your ability to deliver. Don't add filters just because a template has empty boxes.

Build a language bank

Collect the words buyers actually use in calls, emails, support threads, interviews and public discussions. Record the exact phrase, the context, the underlying task and whether you're allowed to publish it. "Every proposal comes back to me" is far more useful than "founder bottleneck optimization."

Ask five people in your audience:

  1. What happened the last time this problem came up?
  2. What did you try?
  3. What made the current approach acceptable until now?
  4. What would improvement change?
  5. What trade-offs would make a solution unattractive?

Five interviews aren't market research. They're a source of better questions and hypotheses. If every answer describes a different problem, narrow the context or rethink the offer.

The relevance filter

Before drafting any post, complete three lines:

  1. "This is for…"
  2. "They recognize the problem when…"
  3. "After reading, they can…"

If line three is just "feel inspired," ask whether that's really the post's purpose. Inspiration has value, but it shouldn't quietly substitute for a practical promise.

Action: ten topics, three keepers

Turn ten broad topics into buyer situations using the three-column table. Keep the three you can explain with evidence. Show one to a target reader without your audience statement: can they tell who it's for? If not, it's still too generic.

Field rule: Smaller audience, better audience. Write for the person who would pay.

Chapter 10: The Authority Equation

Don't tell people you're an expert. Show them how you think.

Authority is a conclusion the reader reaches about your ability to help. Declaring yourself an expert does almost nothing to create it. Showing how you investigate a problem, choose between options and explain the limits gives the reader something to evaluate.

Experience + Evidence + Insight = Authority
Experience
Real contact with the work
Evidence
Something the reader can inspect
Insight
Why the evidence matters

Instead of "I'm an expert in sales," show something like "We tested four outbound approaches across 137 opportunities. Here's what happened." (That's the shape of the claim, not a real statistic. Use your own numbers.)

Authority tools, ranked by what they prove

Tool Proves… Watch out for…
Documented result You've produced outcomes like this Comparability to the reader's situation; permission
Process demonstration How you work Making it concrete enough to evaluate
Artifact (a redacted audit, decision matrix or checklist) Your method is real Client confidentiality
Experiment You test rather than guess Small samples; confounders
Mistake / lesson learned Judgment and honesty Turning it into disguised bragging
Strong opinion with a mechanism You understand cause and effect Opinions without a "because"
Behind-the-scenes observation Proximity to the work Oversharing
Framework You can simplify complexity A diagram doesn't validate itself

New practitioners: don't manufacture results to look experienced. Analyze a public example (with clear limits), build a demonstration with sample data, document a small project you actually completed, or publish a reasoned comparison. Say what the evidence shows and what it doesn't. That honesty is an authority signal.

The evidence capsule

For any results post, include six things: context, baseline, action, time period, how you defined the outcome, and a limitation.

  • Weak: "We increased conversions by 40%."
  • Stronger (if true): "In a four-week test, completed inquiry forms rose from 10 of 200 visits to 14 of 200. Small sample, and the traffic mix may have changed, so we can't credit the rewrite for all of it."

That's a 40% relative increase and a two-percentage-point increase, and knowing the difference is itself a credibility signal. (Hypothetical numbers, used only to show the structure.)

Strong opinions need a mechanism

"More tools won't fix your operations" is familiar and forgettable. "If two teams define a 'qualified lead' differently, a shared dashboard just displays their disagreement faster" explains how the problem happens. Follow the mechanism with a decision rule ("agree the definition and owner before choosing dashboard fields"), and the reader can apply your thinking and judge it.

Handle thin evidence honestly

Use "in this example," "my working hypothesis" or "the client reported" when there's a real limit, not as decoration on an exaggerated claim. If the uncertainty undermines your main promise, change the promise.

Remember what each kind of evidence proves. A framework diagram doesn't validate a framework. A screenshot doesn't establish cause. A testimonial doesn't prove typical results.

Action: the proof ledger

Create a ledger with columns for claim, source, date, permission, limitations and approved wording. Add five claims you could publish today. Delete any for which you can't find the underlying record. (It's a tab in the Content Engine Tracker.)

Field rule: Authority is shown, not stated. Every claim needs a receipt.

Chapter 11: The Problem-Awareness Ladder

Two people can have the same problem and need completely different posts.

One reader hasn't noticed the problem yet. Another has compared providers and wants to know whether your implementation fits their team. Giving both the same educational introduction wastes everyone's attention.

Ready to buy"Who the implementation sprint is for, and what it requires"
Provider aware"What a sales-handoff audit actually includes"
Solution aware"Decision rules vs. another sales hire"
Problem aware"3 reasons your pipeline dries up every quarter"
Unaware"Your sales team might not have a lead problem"

Figure 3. The Problem-Awareness Ladder. A planning aid: people skip rungs, go backward, and sit on different rungs for different parts of a purchase.

Reader state The post's job Example Next step
Unaware Make a symptom recognizable "Why a busy founder can still be the slowest stage in sales" Check one workflow
Problem aware Explain causes and consequences "Three reasons proposals wait for founder input" Use a diagnostic
Solution aware Compare approaches "How we built predictable outbound without hiring 10 SDRs" Compare options
Provider aware Show fit and evidence "What changed after we rebuilt a client's outbound system" Review a sample
Ready to buy Clarify scope and decision "We're taking on [real number] implementation projects this quarter for B2B teams with founder-dependent sales" Discuss the project

(Only state capacity limits that are real. Fake scarcity is a trust leak.)

One problem, climbing the ladder

Suppose you help service businesses reduce onboarding delays:

  • Unaware: a story showing how small access delays pile up.
  • Problem aware: a way to tell client-caused delay from internal handoff failure.
  • Solution aware: automation vs. process redesign vs. account ownership: when each fits.
  • Provider aware: your deliverables, your boundaries, a sample output.
  • Ready to buy: timing, pricing logic, responsibilities, decision process.

Education doesn't always have to come before the offer. Some readers discover your profile when they're already shopping for a provider. Make your commercial information findable, even when most of your feed teaches.

The awareness mismatch

A cold reader who sees "Book your strategy call" doesn't know what problem the call solves. A ready buyer who reads another inspirational post still can't find your scope. Both are matching failures, not writing failures.

The fix isn't a rigid sequence everyone must follow. It's a portfolio with clear routes: a diagnostic post that points to a resource, a case study that points to service details, a profile with an obvious entry point for readers arriving at any stage.

Read signals without overreading them

  • "This happens every month" → problem recognition.
  • "Have you used this with a remote team?" → evaluation.
  • "What would you need from us?" → possible implementation interest.

Each deserves a relevant answer. None of them proves budget, authority or urgency on its own. Answer the question first, then ask one proportionate follow-up. Don't interrogate someone because your funnel diagram says they've "entered a stage." (For how to read these conversations in depth, see The Non-Salesy DM.)

Action: five rungs, one problem

Write five premises for one problem, one per rung, each with a different next step. Check that your ready-to-buy post contains real offer information, and that your unaware post makes sense to someone who's never heard of your framework.

Field rule: Match the post to where the reader is, not to where you want them to be.

Chapter 12: The Four Posts Every Business Needs

Attract → Educate → Prove → Convert → Nurture.

A healthy content strategy isn't "write five viral posts." It's a portfolio of four jobs:

AttractionReach the right new people
AuthorityProve your thinking
RelationshipDeepen connection and community
ConversionMake the next step clear
Job Goal Best engines Success looks like
Attraction New relevant eyeballs Story, contrarian, list, trend Relevant new followers, profile visits from your audience
Authority Trust How-to, case study, lessons learned, data Saves, specific questions, "how would this work for us?"
Relationship Community and retention Conversation, behind the scenes, milestones Substantive replies, returning commenters
Conversion Buying intent Offer with boundaries, commercial FAQ, objection answer Fit conversations, qualified opportunities

A feed of only attraction posts becomes entertaining but commercially vague. A feed of only offers gives strangers no reason to believe you.

A starting mix

For a five-post week: 1 attraction · 2 authority · 1 relationship · 1 conversion. For three posts a week, rotate attraction and relationship while keeping one useful explanation and an occasional clear offer visible.

That's a starting allocation, not a proven ratio. And don't publish five times just to satisfy a calendar. If three good posts leave you time to research, reply and deliver, three is better. Consistency means reliably doing useful work, not keeping a streak alive at any cost.

Topic, engine and job are different things

  • Topic is what you discuss: proposal delays.
  • Engine is how you organize it: a story.
  • Job is why you publish it: authority.

Mixing them up makes your calendar repetitive. You can write several posts on proposal delays with different engines, for different awareness rungs, doing different jobs, without ever repeating the same lesson.

A usable planning record has: audience, problem, awareness rung, job, engine, evidence, CTA and review date. Keep it simple. A content database that takes longer to maintain than the posts is a burden, not a system. (The Content Engine Tracker has exactly these columns and nothing more.)

Sell without apologizing, and without repeating yourself

A direct offer is appropriate whenever you can describe the fit and deliver on the promise. You don't need to apologize for selling. Explain the problem, scope, outcome, requirements and next step. Never fabricate scarcity, and never treat your service as a secret revealed only in DMs.

But if every post ends with the same pitch, even your best educational material starts to feel like advertising. Vary the next step to match the reader's task. Some posts should end with a useful instruction and no request at all.

Action: label your last ten

Label your last ten posts (or ten draft premises) by primary job. Find the missing job and write one post to fill it. Don't rebalance just to hit a percentage. Say which reader need the new post serves.

Field rule: Attract the right people, prove you can help, stay in touch, and make buying easy. Every week.

Part IV · From Viral to Lead

Chapter 13: CTAs That Create Conversations

The CTA should match buyer intent, not your quota.

Most LinkedIn CTAs are terrible: "Agree?" "Thoughts?" "Comment YES." They ask for effort without giving a reason, they produce noisy engagement that says nothing about demand, and LinkedIn has said it's working to reduce exactly this kind of engagement bait.

A call to action is a continuation of the lesson. The more effort it asks for, the more clearly the post must have earned it. Asking for a call at the end of an unrelated motivational story leaves a gap the reader has to bridge alone. Most won't.

The CTA ladder

Commercial"If you're solving this this quarter, message me about a pipeline review."
Conversation / DM"If you're not sure whether it's qualification or ownership, message me the stage where it stalls."
Resource"The one-page review sheet is linked below: use it on your next five proposals."
Experience"When proposals stall in your team, which decision is usually unresolved?"
Application"Check one stalled proposal for an owner, a decision and a date."

Figure 4. The CTA Ladder. Climb it only as far as the post has earned.

  • Application serves readers who aren't ready to engage publicly, which is most of them.
  • Experience invites relevant detail, not agreement. "What's the biggest bottleneck you're seeing?" beats "Thoughts?"
  • Resource says what the resource does and how to get it.
  • Conversation / DM works only if you can actually respond usefully and quickly.
  • Commercial makes it clear this is a paid service. That's honest, and it filters well.

Pick the smallest action that moves the reader's actual task forward. "Smaller" doesn't always mean "a freebie." A buyer with a clear need may prefer your pricing page.

One primary action

A post that asks readers to comment, follow, repost, download, subscribe and book a call has given them six competing instructions and, usually, no reason for any of them. Choose one. Secondary routes can live on your profile.

About keyword CTAs ("Comment 'FRAMEWORK' and I'll send it")

A keyword can be a convenient way to deliver a resource. Don't use one just to inflate your visible comment count. It produces noisy evidence about real demand, and it drifts toward the engagement bait LinkedIn says it's reducing. Where a direct link serves the reader better, use the link. Never make praise, tagging friends or reposting the price of access.

Say what the next step costs

If a resource needs an email, say so. If a call is 20 minutes, say what it's for and what they'll leave with. If an audit is paid, say that before anyone invests time in a sales conversation. Clear expectations may cut raw responses and improve fit, which is the trade you want.

  • Weak: "DM me to transform your business."
  • Better: "Message me if you want the scope for a paid review of where your proposals stall. I'll first check whether your sales process is a fit for it."

Action: three CTAs, one post

For your next post, write an application CTA, a resource CTA and a commercial CTA. Choose the one the body actually earns. If you want the commercial CTA but the post gives no reason to trust the offer, strengthen the evidence, not the urgency.

Field rule: Ask for the smallest next step the post has earned, and make its cost clear.

Chapter 14: The Lead Magnet Post

Don't build a lead magnet that attracts freebie hunters. Build one that advances a buying decision.

Resource posts can generate extraordinary activity. They can also fill your inbox with people who will never buy anything. The difference is almost always the resource.

A useful lead magnet solves a small, real problem next to your paid work. It helps a suitable reader complete a task, diagnose a situation or make a decision. "The 500 Best AI Tools" will attract hundreds of people who don't need your service. "A one-page worksheet to find where your proposals stall" has an obvious relationship to sales-process consulting.

Design backward from the paid service

  1. Write down the paid outcome you deliver.
  2. Identify the decision a buyer must make before they'd consider that service.
  3. Design the resource around that decision.
Paid outcome Precursor decision Good lead magnet Weak lead magnet
Clearer client onboarding (ops consultant) Is the delay access, ownership, scope or scheduling? A handoff checklist A generic productivity ebook
Better interview performance for PM roles (career coach) Where am I actually losing interviews? A structured post-interview reflection sheet Motivational quotes
Predictable outbound pipeline (B2B agency) Is our problem volume, targeting or conversion? A pipeline-leak diagnostic "100 cold email templates"
Fractional CFO engagement Do we understand our runway risk? A 12-month cash-scenario template "10 finance tips for founders"

The five-part resource post

ProblemInsight
(delivered publicly)Promise
what it helps you doContents + fit
who it's for, and not forAccess
clear, honest route

If every proposal needs founder approval, check the decision rules before you hire.

The bottleneck is usually "who can approve what," not capacity.

I built a one-page worksheet with five stages, three ownership states and a next-action field. It helps agency owners pick one handoff to fix first.

It doesn't calculate revenue loss or prescribe a full sales process.

The worksheet is at the link below. No email needed.

Notice the boundary ("it doesn't…"). A one-page resource shouldn't claim to diagnose an entire business. Overpromising can win downloads and lose trust the moment someone opens the file.

Gated or ungated?

  • Ungated when the goal is broad usefulness and low friction.
  • Email-gated when ongoing delivery or a newsletter is genuinely part of the value. Say what they're signing up for, and keep resource access separate from optional promotions.
  • By DM request only when conversation adds value and you can fulfill every request promptly.

Deliver first. "Here's the worksheet you asked for. Start with the stage where work waits longest. If you want to tell me which one you picked, I can help you use it." Never make a discovery call the price of a resource you promised.

Measure the resource, not the downloads

Downloads show demand for access, not demand for your service. Track successful delivery, observable use, relevant questions, fit conversations and opportunities. After a sensible interval, you can ask one optional practical question ("Were you able to pick one handoff to review?"). Don't send repeated reminders to people who never asked for support.

Action: the resource spec

Write a spec: user, task, inputs, output, time required, limitation, delivery method, connection to your paid service. Give a draft to two target users and watch where they hesitate. Fix the instructions before you promote it.

Field rule: The best lead magnet is the first step of the work you get paid for.

Chapter 15: Turning Comments Into Conversations

A viral post creates attention. Your comment section creates relationships.

Your replies show how you treat people who aren't paying you. They also reveal whether your expertise holds up outside a prepared post. A thoughtful comment deserves a reply to its substance, not an automatic invitation to your calendar.

Classify the comment first

Comment contains… Respond with…
Appreciation A genuine thank-you. That's enough.
A specific experience A follow-up question that narrows the situation
Disagreement A clarification, a correction, or a concession if they're right
A resource request Fulfillment, promptly
A buying question A direct commercial answer
  • Bad: "Thanks! DM me if interested."
  • Better: "Interesting that you mentioned hiring. Is the bigger issue getting enough candidates, or finding ones with the right experience?"

Now you're having a conversation.

Respond with context

Reader: This keeps happening after procurement gets involved.

Author: Does the delay usually come from new requirements, or from waiting on approval of what was already agreed?

The question narrows things without claiming to know the cause. If they answer, contribute something useful before asking anything else. Don't turn the thread into a questionnaire.

Reader: What do you charge for this?

Author: It depends on scope. Happy to explain the standard review and what changes the price. Would you prefer the details here or by message?

If you have a published price, just share it. Don't hide a simple answer behind an unnecessary call.

Buying signals, and what they don't prove

Signals worth noticing: the reader describes the problem in their own business, asks how something would work for them, asks about process, timing or price, or asks to talk. Each deserves a direct, relevant answer. None of them proves budget, authority or urgency on its own. Interest is not readiness.

Moving to DM

Move to private messages when the person asks, when the context becomes sensitive, or when a specific exchange would be easier there. Ask first: "This might involve details you'd rather not post publicly. Want to continue by message?" A public comment is not blanket permission for a sales sequence.

Your first DM should carry the shared context: "You mentioned proposals stall after procurement joins. Happy to help think it through. Is it new requirements or approval timing?" If they already answered that publicly, don't ask again.

A complete illustrative exchange

Commenter: We have an account manager, but everything still comes back to me.

Author: Which decisions come back most often: scope changes, pricing or client escalations?

Commenter: Mostly scope. Nobody wants to commit without checking.

Author: That's worth looking at as a decision rule. A job title doesn't say what someone can approve. Do you have written boundaries for small changes?

Commenter: Not written down. Can I message you?

Author (DM): Of course. Start with one recent request and what made it hard to approve. You can leave client details out.

Once context is shared, the commercial transition offers a real choice: "The immediate step looks like defining which changes your account manager can approve. If you want help implementing that across the team, I can explain the paid review. If you just need a starting point, the worksheet covers the first decision." It follows an expressed problem, and it doesn't pretend the commenter has already decided to buy.

Follow-up boundaries

If you promised a resource, send it. If you agreed a date, follow up on that date. If a conversation stops without an agreement, one relevant check-in after a few business days is reasonable ("Checking whether you still wanted the scope for the review. If priorities moved, no need to continue"). After a decline, stop. Silence isn't a hidden objection you're entitled to overcome.

Where this book hands off

Everything after "Can I message you?" (reading the buyer's state, recognizing which trust question they're answering, choosing the smallest next move, knowing when not to send) is the subject of my companion book, The Non-Salesy DM. This book gets the right conversations started. That one helps you handle them without pressure.

Action: five replies

Draft replies to five comment types: appreciation, disagreement, a problem description, a resource request and a price question. Each reply must answer what was actually said before it tries to move anything forward.

Field rule: Reply to the substance, not the opportunity.

Chapter 16: The Profile-to-Post Conversion System

The post makes a claim about your thinking. The profile has to confirm it.

Someone reads your post. Then, often:

Read postClick profileRead headlineScan AboutCheck FeaturedDecide whether to contact you

People skip steps and browse in different orders, so treat this as a design model, not a law. But the requirement is universal: coherence. If your posts discuss agency sales processes and your profile lists six unrelated services, the reader has to do the work of figuring out your relevance. Most won't bother.

Headline

Audience + problem or outcome + method or role.

"Helping B2B agency owners reduce founder dependence in sales | Qualification, proposal and follow-up systems."

Avoid stacking fashionable titles with no connecting idea. A reader shouldn't have to reconcile six identities to understand what you want to be known for.

Banner

Reinforce a memorable problem or principle rather than repeating the headline. "Where does your pipeline wait for you?" Keep it legible, and check that your profile photo doesn't cover the important part on mobile.

About section

A practical structure:

  1. "You may be here because…" followed by two recognizable situations.
  2. "The work focuses on…" followed by scope.
  3. "My approach…" followed by process.
  4. "Evidence…" followed by verified proof or an honest sample.
  5. "Next step…" followed by one clear route.

Plain paragraphs. Specific achievements only when you can support them.

Featured and the contact path

Pick a small set of assets with distinct jobs: an entry resource, evidence of your method, service details. Label them by reader value. "Proposal handoff worksheet" beats "My latest PDF."

Then check every destination on your phone. A broken link, an unreadable page, a vague contact form or a resource that never arrives can waste all the attention your writing earned. The conversion path includes what happens after the click.

The stranger test

Show your profile to someone who hasn't heard your pitch. Give them 20 seconds, then ask:

  1. Who is this for?
  2. What problem does this person solve?
  3. What makes that believable?
  4. What would you do next?

Their answers are worth far more than "does it look professional?"

Action: the coherence trace

Put one recent post, your headline, your About section and your first destination link side by side. Underline the shared buyer problem. If it changes at every step, pick one coherent path and fix it before you drive more traffic.

Field rule: Every click after the post should say the same thing the post said.

Chapter 17: From Content to Client

Content reduces uncertainty before a conversation. It can't replace the conversation.

A lead engine needs a commercial process that can handle the interest it creates. Four checks tell you whether a conversation is worth evaluating further: problem, fit, decision path and next step. You need enough information to decide, not a fully completed qualification form.

Qualify through relevant questions

  • Problem: "What's happening now, and what does it interrupt?"
  • Fit: "Which part would you want help changing?"
  • Decision path: "Who else would need to evaluate a project like this?"
  • Timing: "Is this something you want to address soon, or are you collecting options?"

Ask about resources in context, and share your commercial frame first: "The standard engagement is in this fee range and needs these people involved. Is that realistic for what you have in mind?" Never withhold your price while asking someone to disclose their budget.

Someone without budget right now can still be a valuable relationship. They just aren't an opportunity yet. Record the difference, and never treat them dismissively.

Discovery calls with an outcome

Before inviting a call, say what it will resolve: "A 20-minute conversation would let us map where proposals wait, check whether it's in scope, and decide whether a review makes sense." Offer a written alternative when the questions can be answered that way.

During the call, cover the current state, the desired change, constraints, previous attempts and the decision process. Reflect back your understanding. Give your recommendation with its boundaries. End with an agreed action, an owner and a date, or a clear decision not to proceed.

Objections are information

They say A useful response
"We can do this internally." "That may be the right choice. The worksheet gives you a start. Outside help is most useful when capacity, cross-team decisions or implementation are the blocker. Do any of those apply?"
"It's too expensive." "Is it the available budget, the scope, or uncertainty about the value? If budget's the constraint, let's be direct about it."
"Send me information." "Sure. I'll send scope, requirements, fee and a sample output. Is there one question you need it to answer?"
"Not now." "Understood. Is there a point when a reminder would help, or would you rather come back to it yourself?" Then honor the answer.

Reduce scope only when the smaller engagement still works. Never promise the same work at an arbitrary discount.

Close with a clear agreement

A proposal connects the buyer's situation to deliverables, responsibilities, schedule, fee, payment terms, exclusions and acceptance steps. Don't turn a hoped-for business result into a guarantee you can't control. Specify the work you'll deliver and the outcomes you'll measure together. A verbal yes isn't a completed sale: follow the agreed contracting and payment process, then deliver the first promised step.

An end-to-end example (illustrative)

  1. A consultant who helps small B2B agencies fix sales handoffs posts about why proposals stall after a positive call. An agency founder saves it but doesn't comment.
  2. A later post compares two causes: unclear commercial fit vs. unclear decision ownership. The founder realizes several deals are waiting on internal approval, not another price revision.
  3. A third post offers a worksheet for reviewing five recent opportunities. The founder requests it. The consultant records a resource request, not an opportunity, and delivers it with an offer to help them use it.
  4. The founder replies: "Three of the five have no agreed review date. We keep sending reminders." Now there's a substantive conversation about a real problem. The consultant suggests a small fix the team can try on its own.
  5. The founder asks whether the consultant can make that consistent across the team. The consultant shares the paid review's scope, fee, participation and exclusions. The founder confirms it's a priority and brings in the operations lead. Now it's a qualified opportunity.
  6. On the call, the consultant learns the team also needs a complex CRM migration, which is outside scope. They separate it rather than quietly absorbing it. The narrower scope is accepted, and the proposal records deliverables, responsibilities, timing and terms.
  7. Afterward, the consultant asks what prompted the inquiry. The founder mentions all three posts and a peer's recommendation. The record notes content influence and the referral. It doesn't claim the resource post alone produced the sale.

This is one progression, not a required sequence. Some buyers arrive asking about price on day one. Others use the worksheet and never need paid help. The engine works when every step serves the actual situation.

Action: the opportunity record

Create a one-page record: source post or referral, buyer situation, fit evidence, open questions, stakeholders, timing, next step, agreed follow-up date and status. If you can't fill in the fit evidence and the next step, it's still a conversation. Don't inflate your pipeline.

Field rule: Content starts the decision. A clear, honest process finishes it.

Part V · Your LinkedIn Lead Engine

Chapter 18: Build Your Content Pillars

A pillar is a durable area of buyer concern, not a label broad enough to hold the internet.

"Business," "mindset" and "marketing" don't help you choose tomorrow's post. Pillars exist so that repetition builds recognition instead of monotony.

Five sources of material

  1. What you know: frameworks, checklists, methods.
  2. What you've experienced: real projects, decisions, mistakes.
  3. What you believe: reasoned positions, including unpopular ones.
  4. What you've learned: how your thinking has changed, and why.
  5. What your customers need: their questions, objections, language.

These are inputs. Translate them into buyer-facing themes before anything goes on the calendar.

From your knowledge to their decisions

For a consultant focused on agency sales, pillars might be:

  1. Diagnosing pipeline problems
  2. Clarifying the offer
  3. Improving sales-to-delivery handoffs
  4. Reducing founder dependence
  5. Evaluating implementation choices

Each pillar draws on all five sources. "What I know" produces a qualification checklist. "What I experienced" supplies a real handoff story. "What I believe" supports an argument against premature automation. "What I learned" explains a revised process. "What customers need" reveals the next objection to address.

Don't create a pillar just because you enjoy the topic. Keep a little room for broader interests if they support your professional identity. But the more unrelated territory you cover, the harder it is for a new reader to remember what you do.

The problem bank

Keep a simple bank with five fields: buyer phrase, situation, decision, available evidence, possible next step. Capture entries right after calls and delivery work, while the context is fresh.

Example record. Buyer phrase: "We get inquiries, but most want something cheaper." Situation: a specialist agency attracting early-stage businesses. Decision: change targeting, offer or qualifying information? Evidence: interview notes and inquiry categories. Next step: check the promise in the lead magnet and profile.

That one record can become an attraction post about the symptom, an authority post comparing causes, a relationship question about trade-offs and a conversion post describing a focused review. Same problem, four different jobs.

Repurpose by changing the decision

Repurposing should add a new use, not just reformat the same sentences. Turn a case into a diagnostic, the diagnostic into a demonstration, the demonstration into an objection answer, and the objection into an implementation guide. When you revisit a topic, bring a new example, boundary, question or piece of evidence.

A weekly research habit

Spend one short session a week reviewing buyer language, completed work, unanswered comments and changes in your field. Select ideas by audience relevance and evidence strength. A good idea bank contains plenty of material you're choosing not to publish yet.

Action: five pillars

Create five buyer-facing pillars. Under each, write three decisions a customer faces and two evidence sources you can access. Remove any pillar that can't produce both a useful post and a plausible connection to your work. (The Content Engine Tracker's Problem Bank tab has these fields.)

Field rule: Pillars are the problems you want to be remembered for solving.

Chapter 19: The 30-Day Lead Plan

The first month builds a working process and an evidence base. It's too short to promise revenue.

Treat your first 30 days as the first learning cycle of an ongoing system. B2B buying cycles are often longer than a month. So judge it by whether the engine works, and let the commercial results mature.

Choose your cadence

Standard (3 posts/week) Intensive (5 posts/week)
Posts in 30 days 12 20
Best for Consultants with delivery work; first-time systematic posters Operators with time and material to spare
Weekly mix 1 attraction · 1 authority · 1 relationship or conversion 1 attraction · 2 authority · 1 relationship · 1 conversion

Intensive weekly rhythm: Monday, story (attraction) · Tuesday, how-to (authority) · Wednesday, contrarian (attraction/authority) · Thursday, case study or demonstration (authority) · Friday, resource or offer (conversion). Swap one slot for a conversation post (relationship) when you need it.

If you publish fewer posts, extend the sequence rather than squeezing out the research and evidence checks. A slower system you can maintain beats an ambitious calendar you abandon in week two.

The Standard four-week sequence

Week Purpose Posts Supporting work
1 Establish relevance Day 5 symptom · Day 7 method · Day 9 field question Audience, profile, baseline, proof ledger
2 Demonstrate judgment Day 12 comparison · Day 14 case/demonstration · Day 16 resource Build and test the resource; handle replies
3 Connect interest to fit Day 19 objection answer · Day 21 lesson learned · Day 23 offer Review conversations and the commercial path
4 Improve from evidence Day 25 sharper field question · Day 27 method variation · Day 29 commercial FAQ Diagnose results; design the next cycle

Chapter 26 turns this into daily assignments.

Run one experiment

Start with one question, such as: "Do posts about proposal ownership attract more fit conversations than broad sales advice?" Keep the audience and offer consistent, vary the example and engine, and track both reach and the nature of responses.

Don't change audience, positioning, frequency, format, offer and CTA all at once and then claim you found "the best hook." You won't know what worked.

Plan your response capacity

Before a resource post, estimate how many requests you can fulfill and how fast. Prepare the resource, the access instructions and the delivery message, and test the link on a phone. Before an offer post, make sure you can deliver the scope and onboard a client. If capacity is limited, say so honestly. Never invent a scarcity story.

A sustainable time budget
