A starting week: 45 minutes of research, two 60-minute drafting and editing sessions, three short reply sessions, 30 minutes of review. Track your actual time for two weeks before deciding whether content is "worth it." If you only have 90 minutes a week, publish one strong post, reply carefully and review a few signals.

Action: put it on the calendar

Put your publication dates and four review sessions on your calendar now. Give each post a buyer problem, a primary job, an evidence source and a CTA. If any field is unknown, resolving it becomes a task before publication.

Field rule: Consistency means reliably doing useful work, not keeping a streak alive.

Chapter 20: The Post Creation Workflow

Separate finding, drafting, editing, publishing and learning.

Mixing these creates friction: you research while polishing a sentence, invent a hook before you know the point, and check analytics while trying to finish the body. Here's the workflow in fifteen steps.

The 15-Step Workflow
# Step What "done" looks like
Find
1 Find the problem A specific buyer situation from your problem bank: who has it, and when
2 Find the insight The explanation or decision rule in one sentence. "This is important" doesn't count.
3 Find the story or demonstration Evidence that supports the insight. If there's no true story, use a labeled hypothetical or a process.
4 Write ten hooks Varied angles, each a promise the evidence can keep
Build
5 Choose the strongest hook Clear relevance and a deliverable promise beat theatrical language
6 Write the rehook Adds context, tension or a preview; no repeated meaning
7 Build the body Pick an engine; each paragraph answers the question the last one raised
8 Add proof Example, artifact, source or measurement details, with permission and limits checked
9 Add the payoff What the reader now understands or can do; it resolves the hook
10 Write the CTA Matches awareness and the post's job. No CTA beats an irrelevant one.
Ship and learn
11 Remove fluff Unsupported superlatives, repeated claims and self-praise gone
12 Format for mobile Preview it; the opening makes sense on its own; links clearly labeled
13 Publish Right account, audience, attachments and destination; timed for your readers and your availability to reply
14 Engage Answer relevant questions; correct misunderstandings; never fake activity
15 Analyze Consistent observation window; metrics and conversation quality; the next question this post revealed

The ten-line post brief

Before writing, fill in: reader · situation · awareness rung · primary job · thesis · engine · evidence · boundary · payoff · CTA. Ten lines can save an hour of unfocused editing.

Example brief. Reader: agency founder. Situation: proposals need founder approval. Awareness: problem aware. Job: authority. Thesis: unclear decision rights may be creating the queue. Engine: how-to. Evidence: sample decision matrix. Boundary: doesn't fix poor offer fit. Payoff: define approval rules for one recurring request type. CTA: apply the check to a recent proposal.

The quality gate (V.A.L.U.E.)

Before publishing, mark each as ready / revise / unknown:

  • Visibility: Can the intended reader recognize the subject in the opening?
  • Attention: Does the rehook add meaning, and does the body keep the promise?
  • Legitimacy: Are claims supported, examples labeled, limits proportionate?
  • Usefulness: Can the reader make a better decision or complete a task?
  • Engagement-to-Action: Is the next step clear, appropriate and working?

Don't add the marks up into a pretend virality score. Fix every "unknown" fact and every broken destination before you publish. A beautiful phrase doesn't make up for a missing explanation.

Action: time one post

Run one idea through all fifteen steps without skipping the proof check. Record the time each phase takes. If drafting is slow because evidence is missing, improve how you capture it. If editing is slow because the thesis keeps changing, improve the brief.

Field rule: Don't write a hook until you know the point.

Chapter 21: Measuring What Actually Matters

Measure the business without inventing attribution.

Measurement exists to help you decide what to do next. A dashboard full of activity counts can distract from that job. Start with a small set of clearly defined measures, and keep the definitions stable long enough to compare them.

LinkedIn's own analytics define impressions as the number of times a post was shown and members reached as the distinct members who saw it. LinkedIn describes these as estimates, and some counts can include repeat or your own activity. Check the current definitions in your analytics before comparing numbers.

Three layers

Layer Measures What it tells you What it doesn't
Distribution Impressions, members reached, audience data Exposure Whether viewers fit
Response Relevant comments, substantive DMs, resource use, profile and link activity Interest and friction Buyer qualification
Commercial progression Fit conversations, qualified opportunities, proposals, won work, cash collected Business results Which single post "caused" it

A like is a lighter signal than a detailed description of a problem, and neither automatically qualifies anyone.

Define the denominator

  • Fit conversation rate = fit conversations ÷ substantive new conversations. (Six of twelve = 50%. It is not six divided by every reaction and impression.)
  • Opportunity rate = qualified opportunities ÷ fit conversations.
  • Proposal win rate = won ÷ decided proposals. Report open proposals separately.
  • Landing-page conversion = completed resource requests ÷ measured page sessions. Don't silently swap in LinkedIn link clicks.

Always state the time period and cohort, especially when decisions happen weeks after the post.

An Illustrative Monthly Record (invented for instruction; not a benchmark)
Measure Count What it means
Posts published 12 Output, not success
Substantive new conversations 12 People discussing a real issue
Fit conversations 6 Relevant audience and problem
Qualified opportunities 3 Fit + decision path + agreed next step
Proposals sent 2 A commercial proposal made sense
Won 1 Met your documented win definition
Open 1 Still undecided. Not a loss.

Track contribution, not sole cause

Ask every new prospect how they found you and what made them reach out. Record the first known touch, any content they mention, the immediate trigger and other channels involved. Real paths look like this: a post, a referral, several articles, then a reply to an email. Report sourced and influenced opportunities separately, under definitions you write down, and never credit the full deal to every channel that touched it.

Revenue isn't profit. Compare cash collected with delivery costs and with the time content and conversations take. Pipeline value isn't cash either, and an arbitrary close probability doesn't make it cash.

Diagnose the pattern

Pattern Likely area to inspect
Low reach, but relevant responses Distribution or audience size
High reach, poor fit Topics too broad; positioning drift
Relevant profile visits, little contact Offer clarity or next step
Many resource requests, little use The promise, the audience or the resource itself
Calls with poor fit Qualification or targeting

These are hypotheses. Read actual examples before changing the system. One bad week can be normal variation, timing or a slow buying cycle.

Review rhythm

Take an early snapshot for operational issues, and a consistent later one (say, seven days after publishing) for comparison. Review commercial progression monthly and by cohort over your buying cycle. Keep older posts attached to opportunities they later influence, rather than declaring their value over after a week.

Action: set up the record

Track post ID, audience, job, evidence, responses, opportunities and time spent. (The Content Engine Tracker's Metrics tab calculates these rates for you.) Choose your next experiment from the biggest documented bottleneck.

Field rule: Measure qualified attention. Everything else is a leading indicator at best.

Chapter 22: 50 Hook Templates

Structures for an idea you can support. Replace the brackets with a real audience, situation or fact.

A hook is ready only when the body can keep its promise. The examples show wording, not verified results. First-person versions require your own true experience.

Problem hooks
# Template Example

# Template Example

Use the library deliberately. Choose five hooks for the same idea, not five ideas for a hook you like. Remove any that misrepresent the evidence. Record which opening helped readers understand the topic. Reach alone can't tell you why a post worked. (All 50 are pre-loaded in the Content Engine Tracker's Hook Bank.)

Add context
# Template Example

Adaptable drafting templates: a primary job, the inputs you need, a body structure and a sensible next step.

These aren't performance-tested promises. Replace every bracket, verify every fact, and choose a CTA that matches your real offer and capacity.

# Structure Primary job Gather first

02 The bounded how-to Authority A task and a completion test

01 · The decision story (Authority)

We expected [outcome].

Then [event] made the plan harder.

The easy answer was [option A]. But [constraint] meant that would leave [problem] unsolved.

We chose [option B] because [reason].

Over [period], we saw [supported result]. We can't credit [uncertain effect] to this alone.

If you're facing [similar condition], check [decision] before [action].

Next step: Invite a comparable experience. Use only with a real story, or label it hypothetical.

02 · The bounded how-to (Authority)

To [task], start by confirming [prerequisite].

First, [action]. Next, [action]. Then, [action].

Check it worked by [observable test]. If [failure condition], go back to [step].

This helps with [scope]. It won't fix [separate problem].

Next step: Ask readers to try it on one real item. Avoid vague verbs like "optimize."

03 · The diagnostic list (Attraction / authority)

[Problem] doesn't always mean [assumed cause].

Check these three signals:

  1. [Signal] → check [possible cause].
  2. [Signal] → check [possible cause].
  3. [Signal] → check [possible cause].

Start with the one you can see in [recent example]. The point is to narrow the diagnosis before you buy a solution.

Next step: Offer a worksheet only if it helps perform the check.

04 · The qualified contrarian (Authority)

"[Common advice]" is useful when [condition].

It becomes weak advice when [constraint].

Here's why: [mechanism].

In that situation, I'd choose [alternative] first, because [reason].

If [different condition], the original advice may still be right.

Next step: Ask which condition readers are in. Don't invent a consensus just to oppose it.

05 · The transparent case study (Authority / conversion)

[Business context] was dealing with [problem].

Starting point: [defined baseline].

We changed [specific action] over [period]. The client's part was [responsibilities].

Result: [defined measure]. [Other change or limitation] also matters when reading that.

The useful lesson is [mechanism], especially for [fit condition].

Next step: Offer a sample scope to similar buyers. Never imply the same result is guaranteed.

06 · The revised belief (Relationship / authority)

I used to believe [old view].

That led me to [action].

After [real observation], I realized I'd overlooked [factor].

Now I check [question] before [decision].

I still use the old approach when [exception]. What changed is how I choose.

Next step: Ask what changed the reader's approach.

07 · The useful failure (Authority)

[Attempt] didn't produce [intended outcome].

My part in that: [specific decision or omission].

The evidence points to [explanation], though [uncertainty] remains.

Next time I'll [changed action] and check [signal] earlier.

If you're about to [similar action], ask [preventive question] first.

Next step: A prevention checklist. Don't use vulnerability as disguised self-congratulation.

08 · The milestone with a lesson (Relationship)

We just reached [verified milestone].

The part worth sharing is [decision or process].

[People or conditions] made it possible. [Constraint] shaped how we worked.

The next challenge is [honest limitation].

If you're working toward [related goal], start with [useful lesson].

Next step: Credit contributors accurately. A milestone doesn't prove every tactic around it caused it.

09 · The trend, translated (Attraction / authority)

[Source] announced [change] on [date].

For [specific audience], the practical implication may be [inference].

Before changing anything, check [factor one] and [factor two].

I'd act now on [clear action], and wait for more evidence on [uncertainty].

Next step: Link the source. Never recycle old news as breaking.

10 · The small-data read (Authority)

In [sample and period], we saw [finding].

That number means [definition]. It doesn't mean [common misreading].

One explanation: [hypothesis]. Another: [alternative].

Next test: [comparison]. For now, the change we're making is [proportionate action].

Next step: Invite questions about method. Small data can guide a next step; it can't support a sweeping claim.

11 · The resource invitation (Conversion: resource)

If [problem], start by checking [insight, delivered in the post].

I made [resource] to help [audience] do [bounded task].

It contains [specific components] and gives you [output].

It's for [context]. It's not for [exclusion].

Get it here: [access route]. [State any email requirement clearly.]

Next step: Deliver exactly what you promised before offering paid help.

12 · The reasoned opinion (Authority / relationship)

My view: [specific position].

The reason: [mechanism].

Take [example]. In that situation, [consequence].

I'd change my mind if [condition or evidence].

The decision I'd make today: [action].

Next step: Ask for counterexamples from similar contexts, not agreement.

13 · The conditional prediction (Attraction / authority)

I expect [development], if [conditions] continue.

The signals I'm watching: [source-backed observations].

For [reader], preparing means [reversible action].

The prediction weakens if [counter-signal]. I wouldn't commit [large irreversible investment] on this alone.

Next step: Name a review date, and actually revisit the forecast.

14 · The mistake and the repair (Authority)

A common way to make [task] harder: [mistake].

It happens for a reasonable reason: [motivation].

The problem is [mechanism], especially when [condition].

Replace it with [specific action]. Check the fix by [test].

Next step: Ask readers to inspect one example. Never mock people for making the mistake.

15 · Behind the scenes (Authority)

Before we [visible deliverable], we decide [less visible question].

Here's what that looks like: [artifact or explanation].

We include [element] because [reason], and leave out [element] because [scope boundary].

That helps [person] make [decision].

Next step: Share a sample if it's safe. Never expose client information for credibility.

16 · The honest transformation (Authority / conversion)

Before: [specific behavior or state].

After: [specific behavior or state].

The change: [intervention], with [required participation].

What we observed: [evidence]. What we haven't established yet: [longer-term outcome].

That distinction matters because [reason].

Next step: Explain implementation fit. Operational clarity is valuable without a fabricated revenue number.

17 · The option comparison (Authority, solution aware)

Choosing between [A] and [B] starts with [decision criterion].

Choose [A] when [condition]. The trade-off: [cost or limit].

Choose [B] when [condition]. The trade-off: [cost or limit].

If [third condition], neither should be your first move. Start with [prerequisite].

Next step: Offer a decision worksheet. Don't rig the comparison so your service always wins.

18 · The objection explained (Authority, provider aware)

"[Objection]" is a reasonable concern when [context].

Here's what [service or method] does address: [scope].

Here's what it doesn't: [limit].

It's worth considering when [fit]. It's probably wrong when [non-fit].

Next step: Invite a specific scope question. Naming non-fit makes the decision clearer, and makes you more believable.

19 · The commercial FAQ (Conversion)

Three questions about [service]:

Who's it for? [Audience and problem.]

What happens? [Deliverables, sequence, client responsibilities.]

What does it cost and require? [Actual fee or honest pricing logic, timing, requirements.]

If that fits your situation, [clear next step].

Next step: Give enough information to evaluate, not just a calendar link.

20 · The myth with a better rule (Attraction / authority)

"[Belief]" leaves out [important condition].

In [example], following it leads to [consequence].

A more useful rule: [bounded recommendation].

Before applying it, check [question].

Next step: Invite cases where the original rule still works.

21 · The annotated teardown (Authority)

This [page / process / message] is trying to help [audience] do [task].

What works: [specific element and why].

What creates friction: [observable element and likely effect].

My first test would be [change], measured by [signal].

This is an outside view. I don't know [missing internal context].

Next step: Share your evaluation criteria. Never present guesses about someone else's results as fact.

22 · The buyer's decision checklist (Authority, solution aware)

Before choosing [provider or approach], ask:

What problem will this solve first?
What inputs and participation does it need?
What evidence would show progress?
What's out of scope?
What happens if the assumptions are wrong?

A clear answer matters more than a confident promise.

Next step: Encourage readers to use it with any provider, including you.

23 · The field question (Relationship)

For [specific audience] dealing with [situation]: how do you handle [decision]?

I can see the case for [A] because [reason], and for [B] because [reason].

My current preference is [view], when [condition].

What have you seen in practice? Context like [non-sensitive detail] would help.

Next step: Reply to the answers, and credit useful contributions with permission.

24 · The offer with boundaries (Conversion)

I help [audience] fix [problem] through [service].

It includes [deliverables] over [period].

You'll need [inputs and participation]. It doesn't include [scope boundary].

The fee is [actual fee or range, with assumptions]. First we check [fit criteria].

If you want to evaluate it, [next step, and what happens after].

Next step: State capacity limits only if they're real. Swap vague transformation promises for concrete work.

25 · The follow-up lesson (Authority / relationship)

I recently wrote about [idea].

The replies raised a useful point: [question or correction].

Here's what I'd clarify now: [revised explanation].

The original advice still holds when [condition]. When [different condition], use [alternative].

The better rule: [rule].

Next step: Link the earlier post. Revising a view in public is stronger than defending an overstatement.

The adaptation check. Before publishing any template: the audience is specific, the evidence is yours or attributed, any promised resource exists, every bracket is replaced, and the CTA matches your capacity. Then read the draft without its template label. It should sound like a real contribution, not a filled-in form.

Chapter 25: The Viral-to-Lead Swipe File

Annotated examples: hook, rehook, structure, trigger, audience, value, CTA and lead mechanism.

The first seven are original worked examples written for this book. They aren't reproductions of anyone's posts, and their performance hasn't been measured. "Viral-to-lead" names the intended path, not a claim that they went viral. After them, I annotate openings from my own feed.

Read each one twice: first as the intended buyer, then as the writer studying the choices.

Example 1 · Agency founder dependence

Your sales process has an availability problem if every proposal waits for you.

A new template won't decide which exceptions your team can approve.

Start with the last proposal that stalled while you were away. What was the team waiting to find out?

Whether the price could change?
Whether the scope was deliverable?
Whether the client was a good fit?

Those are three different decisions. They need three different rules.

Write one boundary for the most common request: who can approve it, within what limits, and when it comes back to you.

Then test that rule on your next real proposal.

Which decision reaches you most often?

Element Analysis
Hook Selects founders who experience proposal delays; reframes it as availability
Rehook Separates document design from decision rights
Structure Diagnostic list → small test
Trigger Recognition of a familiar interruption
Audience / job Agency founders · authority
CTA Experience: invites real operating context
Lead mechanism A founder describing repeated scope escalation may be a fit for process work. Answer their situation first. Someone just agreeing isn't an opportunity.

Example 2 · SaaS onboarding

A welcome email can't fix an unclear first task.

If a new user opens the product and still has to figure out what success means, more reminders just repeat the confusion.

Check the first useful action.

Can the user name it? Do they have what they need to complete it? Does the product show what changed when they're done?

For a reporting tool, that might mean connecting one data source and seeing one meaningful report. For a collaboration tool, it may require a second person to join.

The right first action depends on your product's value, not on how easy it is to count the click.

Before rewriting your email sequence, describe the first useful task in one sentence a new user would understand.

Element Analysis
Hook Challenges an overly narrow fix
Rehook Explains the mechanism
Structure Diagnostic questions + contrasting examples
Audience / job SaaS founders, product and lifecycle teams · authority
CTA Application: no lead capture at all
Lead mechanism The profile carries the onboarding service. A reader asking how to define the first useful task can lead to a scoped conversation. No activation result is claimed.

Example 3 · Specialist freelancer positioning

"I can write anything" makes a buyer do too much work.

They still need to know whether you understand the document they're trying to produce.

A SaaS founder who needs a customer story needs interviews, evidence, approvals and a narrative that helps a buyer evaluate the product.

A founder who needs weekly LinkedIn posts needs a completely different process.

You may be great at both. Your service page should make each one easy to evaluate.

Name the reader, the deliverable, the inputs and what a good result looks like. Show one relevant sample.

Specificity helps because it reduces the buyer's translation work.

Open your profile. Can a stranger identify one document you're especially good at producing?

Element Analysis
Hook Names a positioning habit in the reader's own words
Rehook Names the hidden burden it puts on the buyer
Structure Problem → comparison → decision rule → application
Trigger Self-recognition, not spectacle
Audience / job Specialist freelancers · attraction + authority
Lead mechanism A positioning consultant could connect this to a profile review, but the post is useful without it.

Example 4 · Interview coaching, without inflated promises

Right after an interview, you have a narrow window to capture useful evidence.

"It went badly" is a feeling. It isn't a diagnosis yet.

Write down the questions you remember. Note where you gave a clear example, where you got vague and where the interviewer asked you to clarify.

Then separate preparation gaps from information you simply didn't have.

Couldn't explain a project decision? Practice that explanation. Role needed a skill you haven't used? Decide whether to build it or target a different role.

You can't read the hiring decision from every facial expression.

Use this interview to improve the next one, without pretending you control the employer's choice.

Element Analysis
Hook A timely task with a deadline built in
Rehook Replaces an unhelpful judgment with a diagnostic need
Structure Reflection method + boundary
Audience / job Job candidates · authority
CTA None: the lesson is the ending
Lead mechanism A related post could offer the reflection sheet. A coaching offer must avoid promising job outcomes the coach can't control.

Example 5 · A resource post with clear fit

Before adding another sales meeting, check which decision the current one fails to make.

A longer agenda isn't the same as a clearer outcome.

Take one recurring meeting and write down four things: the decision required, the person responsible, the evidence needed and the deadline.

No decision? It may be an update that belongs in writing. Decision with no owner? Inviting more people may make it worse.

I put those four fields into a one-page meeting review sheet for service-business team leads.

It helps you redesign one recurring meeting. It doesn't prescribe your whole management system.

It's at the link below. No email required.

Element Analysis
Hook + rehook Make a distinction the body then explains
Value delivered publicly The four fields: usable with or without the download
Resource promise Bounded ("one meeting") with an explicit limit
Access Stated clearly (no email)
Lead mechanism Requests to implement decision ownership across teams may indicate consulting fit. Downloads alone don't.

Example 6 · A transparent commercial post

If proposal delays keep pulling you back into sales, a focused process review can show you why.

It covers qualification, proposal prep, decision ownership and follow-up.

We start with a handful of recent opportunities and map where work waited, what information was missing, and who could have moved it forward.

You get a prioritized list of changes, each with an owner and a suggested testing order.

It's for service businesses with an existing offer and an active sales process. It's not a substitute for validating demand from scratch.

You'll need to share suitable records and involve whoever owns sales operations.

If you want the scope, timeline and fee, message me about a proposal-process review.

Element Analysis
Hook Selects by problem, not by title
Rehook Names the scope immediately
Body Method, output, fit, non-fit, participation
CTA Explicitly commercial, with a clear keyword for the DM
Lead mechanism Reply with actual scope, timing and price, and don't make them repeat details they already gave you. Use only for a service you can really deliver.

Example 7 · A relationship post with a real question

Account leads: which client requests can you approve without checking with the founder?

I'm interested in the boundary, not the job title.

A team can have experienced people and still route every small scope change through one person. Sometimes that protects margin. Sometimes the limits have just never been written down.

One useful distinction: a change that fits existing capacity vs. one that changes the delivery commitment.

My starting point would be a short list of changes the account lead can approve, with exceptions reviewed together.

Where does that break down in your team? No client names or sensitive numbers needed.

Element Analysis
Hook Narrows the respondent group precisely
Body Gives a reasoned starting view so respondents aren't doing all the thinking
CTA Invites counterexamples; explicitly protects confidentiality
Lead mechanism The job is relationship and research. A reply should not trigger a pitch. If someone asks for implementation help, evaluate it then.

From my own feed: three openings, annotated

These are real openings from posts I've published. I'm showing them for their structure, not as proof of performance.

We chase reach as if it were the finish line, then wonder where the revenue went.

Attention gets the credit, but the funnel does the work.

Why it's built this way: a contrarian hook aimed at founders and marketers who over-index on reach. The rehook ("attention gets the credit, but the funnel does the work") names the mechanism in one line, which is this book's thesis compressed. The post then used an analogy ("a viral post is a crowd that gathers for ten seconds") to make the abstract concrete.

Most freelancers don't have an income problem.
They have a pipeline problem.

They rely on one source for clients. When that source dries up, so does their income.

Why it's built this way: a problem-reframe hook (#06 in the hook library). It names the reader (freelancers), replaces their framing ("income") with a more useful diagnosis ("pipeline"), and the rehook gives the mechanism in two short sentences. That problem territory sits right next to a service: helping freelancers build a multi-channel pipeline.

"Can we just have a quick call?"

Every consultant has heard this one.

A client books 15 minutes. 15 becomes 30. 30 becomes 45. And somewhere along the way, that "quick call" turns into a full-blown strategy session.

Why it's built this way: a scene hook using the reader's own everyday language. Instant recognition for consultants. The escalating numbers work as a rehook: the reader feels the problem before any lesson arrives. It's a relationship-and-authority post: it builds rapport through shared experience, then earns the right to teach something about scoping and paid advice.

Build your own swipe

Pick one example. Replace its audience, problem, evidence and next step with yours. Label each function in your draft (hook, rehook, body, payoff, CTA). If you can't point to the value delivered before the CTA, revise the body. If your authority depends on a result you haven't achieved, switch to a transparent demonstration.

Chapter 26: Your 30-Day Implementation Challenge

Twelve publishing days. Eighteen days of the research, evidence and review that make publishing work.

This is the daily companion to Chapter 19's Standard plan. The aim is a working lead engine and better judgment, not a promised number of clients. Log every day in the Content Engine Tracker: action, evidence created, reader response, time spent and one adjustment.

Day Task Output
1 Choose the commercial focus: one audience, one recurring problem, one plausible offer, two exclusions Buyer situation statement
2 Collect buyer language: five real phrases, with source and publication permission Five problem-bank records
3 Repair the profile path: headline, About, Featured, contact route; test every link; run the stranger test A coherent path + remaining gaps
4 Build the proof ledger: five honest claims with sources and limits; draft ten hooks for tomorrow Evidence bank + chosen opening
5 ✍️ Publish the symptom post: problem hook + diagnostic list; application or experience CTA Post 1
6 Read the responses: reply; separate appreciation from real problems; add language to the bank Learning note + tomorrow's brief
7 ✍️ Publish a bounded method: how-to with prerequisites and a completion check Post 2
8 Specify the resource: Chapter 14's spec: input, output, limit, access Resource brief
9 ✍️ Publish a field question: context + your view + a specific ask Post 3
10 Review first signals: audience fit, question quality, time spent. Don't change strategy after three posts. Baseline + one question to investigate
11 Build the resource draft: instructions, worked example, clear output; test with two readers A testable resource
12 ✍️ Publish a decision comparison: two legitimate approaches, when each fits Post 4
13 Prepare a case or demonstration: run the evidence capsule check Tomorrow's draft
14 ✍️ Publish the proof post: readable visuals, attributable results Post 5
15 Test fulfillment: full access path on another device; delivery message ready A working resource route
16 ✍️ Publish the resource post: five-part structure; value delivered in the post Post 6
17 Support use: fulfill requests; ask one optional practical question Resource-improvement note
18 Identify fit conversations: check each against problem, fit, decision path, next step An honest conversation list
19 ✍️ Publish an objection answer: when the concern is valid, what you cover, when you're the wrong fit Post 7
20 Prepare the offer details: scope, deliverables, timeline, inputs, exclusions, price, next step A reviewable offer description
21 ✍️ Publish a lesson learned: a real revised belief, or what this cycle is teaching you Post 8
22 Rehearse the conversation path: replies to a price question, an unclear problem, an info request, a polite no A response guide (not a script)
23 ✍️ Publish the offer: fit, scope, requirements, a clear evaluation step Post 9
24 Repair the biggest friction: trace one real path from post to profile to resource or conversation One documented fix
25 ✍️ Publish a sharper field question: compare the discussion with Day 9's Post 10
26 Draft a method variation: a new application, not a reworded repeat Tomorrow's draft
27 ✍️ Publish the improved method: same success definition as the earlier comparable post Post 11
28 Review the commercial record: conversations, fit, opportunities, proposals, wins, losses An accurate pipeline snapshot
29 ✍️ Publish a commercial FAQ: who it's for, what happens, what it requires, how pricing works Post 12
30 Design the next cycle: one problem to continue, one habit to stop, one experiment to run Your next 30-day plan

Intensive track: add the Monday-story and Wednesday-contrarian slots from Chapter 19 on non-publishing days, drawing from the hook library and post structures.

Completion review

  • ☐ A clear audience and problem guided the feed.
  • ☐ The profile and offer support the same promise.
  • ☐ Twelve posts were published, or rescheduled for a stated reason.
  • ☐ Every factual claim has a source or a stated limitation.
  • ☐ The resource works, and access expectations are clear.
  • ☐ Replies responded to context, not a blind sequence.
  • ☐ Opportunities are distinguished from general engagement.
  • ☐ The next experiment targets observed friction.

Review notes. Answer each with an example from the month: the problem that earned the most relevant discussion; the evidence that helped someone evaluate you; where the reader's journey broke; one habit to stop; your next experiment and its review date.

Conclusion: Stop Going Viral. Start Becoming Unmissable.

A lead engine is a sequence of credible experiences. The post makes a problem clearer. The profile confirms your relevance. The resource helps with a real task. The conversation respects context. The offer explains the work. Delivery keeps the promise.

You can improve every one of those experiences without predicting your next viral post. That's where your control lives.

You don't need millions of followers to generate serious business from LinkedIn. I don't have them. You need the ability to consistently earn attention from the right people, show that you understand their problems, and give them a good reason to start a conversation.

So start small and specific. One audience. One problem worth understanding. Write from evidence. Make the opening clear, the body useful and the next step appropriate. Pay attention to what readers reveal. When interest becomes a real opportunity, evaluate it honestly. When it doesn't, leave the person with something useful anyway.

Don't try to become a LinkedIn influencer.

Become the person your ideal buyers already trust before they ever speak to you.

Your next action is concrete: complete the buyer and offer brief, choose one problem, and draft a post that helps someone make a better decision today.

Worksheet 3: The V.A.L.U.E. Edit

Check Question Ready / Revise / Unknown

Don't add up the marks into a pretend virality score. Fix every "unknown" fact and every broken destination before you publish.

The pre-publication checklist

  • ☐ One recognizable reader and one primary job.
  • ☐ The opening promises only what the body delivers.
  • ☐ Every example is real, attributed or clearly labeled illustrative.
  • ☐ Numbers include enough context to read them honestly.
  • ☐ Client information and quotes have permission.
  • ☐ The lesson includes a useful action or decision rule.
  • ☐ The CTA matches the reader's likely task and your capacity.
  • ☐ The resource or commercial destination works on mobile.
  • ☐ No bracketed template instructions remain.

The Common Mistakes Repair Sheet

Mistake Why it hurts First repair
Broad hooks unrelated to your offer Attention with little buyer relevance Rewrite around a recognizable buyer situation
Unsupported result claims Weakens credibility; misleads Add evidence, qualify or remove
Every post asks for a call Asks for more effort than the post earned Match the CTA rung to awareness
Resource requests counted as leads Free-item demand inflates the pipeline Separate requests, conversations and opportunities
Engagement-bait CTAs ("Agree?") Noisy signal; works against relevance Ask for experience or application instead
Blind DM sequences after comments Ignores context and boundaries Reply to the actual signal
A confusing profile Readers can't connect the post to a service Align audience, problem, evidence and next step
Constantly changing strategy Results become unreadable Hold one focus for a full cycle
Copying first-person templates Fiction presented as personal evidence Use real history or a transparent demonstration
Measuring only impressions Exposure mistaken for progress Track fit and commercial progression
Publishing beyond capacity Research, replies and delivery suffer Post less; protect quality
Engagement pods / manufactured comments Inauthentic, and LinkedIn says it acts against it Distribute through real relevance and collaboration

Glossary

Attribution: the method you use to describe a channel's contribution to an outcome; limited by what you can observe.
Authority: the reader's reasoned confidence in your ability to help, built from experience, evidence and insight.
Awareness ladder: unaware → problem aware → solution aware → provider aware → ready to buy.
CTA ladder: application → experience → resource → conversation → commercial.
Engine: a reusable way of organizing an idea: story, how-to, list, contrarian, trend, lessons learned, conversation.
Evidence capsule: context, baseline, action, period, outcome definition, limitation.
Fit conversation: a substantive exchange with someone whose context and problem plausibly match your service.
Hook / rehook / payoff: the opening that earns attention; the passage that makes it worth continuing; the insight that keeps the promise.
Influenced vs. sourced opportunity: an opportunity a channel contributed to vs. one assigned to it under a documented origin rule.
Lead magnet: a useful resource that solves a bounded task next to your paid work.
L.E.A.D.: Lead, Engagement, Alignment, Discovery: the work after the post.
Post jobs: attraction, authority, relationship, conversion.
Qualified attention: attention from people whose situation makes your expertise relevant.
Qualified opportunity: a relevant problem, plausible fit, a credible decision path and an agreed next step.
Substantive conversation: an exchange with enough context to discuss a real problem, beyond a reaction or compliment.
V.A.L.U.E.: Visibility, Attention, Legitimacy, Usefulness, Engagement-to-Action: the final edit.
V.I.R.A.L.: Voice, Intrigue, Relevance, Authority, Lesson: the work inside the post.
